https://www.slugmag.com/arts/film/film-r.text: Image courtesy of Salt Lake Film Society SLFS Summer Showdown: Jojo Rabbit vs. Isle of Dogs By Braxtyn Birrell August 10, 2026 SHARE THIS: Facebook Twitter Film Jojo Rabbit is a very light movie about very heavy things, like World War II. Johannes Betzler ( Roman Griffin Davis , The Long Walk ), a 10-year-old German boy, wants nothing more than to be a Nazi. His imaginary friend, Adolf (played by Jewish director Taika Waititi , What We Do in the Shadows, Thor: Ragnarok ), is there to hype him up when he has doubts about himself or his mission. Left behind by his father who is fighting in the war, he lives with his mother, a playful, engaging and mysterious woman ( Scarlett Johansson , The Avengers ). During a highly anticipated weekend of Nazi training for little boys, he earns the nickname “Jojo Rabbit” after refusing to snap a rabbit’s neck. Embarrassed by his cowardice and emboldened by imaginary Hitler, Jojo grabs hold of a hand grenade and throws it, but when it hits a tree and bounces back on him, he is left deformed and disabled (at least that’s his perspective – in reality, he’s still so cute, and it’s just a slight limp). Taking a break from school due to the accident, he spends much more time at home, hearing noises in his late sister’s bedroom. Eventually, he realizes his mother has hidden a Jewish girl, Elsa ( Thomasin McKenzie , Last Night in Soho ), in their walls. At first, Jojo is terrified of Elsa, believing she is a monster he must slay. But the more time he spends with her, he realizes she is just a person, and he is not a killer. The film ends with the Germans losing the war, and Jojo and Elsa dancing in the street to celebrate her newfound freedom. Jojo Rabbit was a laugh-out-loud movie that at times made me wonder whether I should be laughing. Yet, I don’t think it discredits the seriousness of the Holocaust, rather shines light on how absurd war is. The true consequences of the war were finally brought home after the hanging of Jojo’s mother, but even then, it didn’t hit as hard as you might expect. The tone shift from Jojo Rabbit to Isle of Dogs was palpable. The theatre cleared substantially, and I won two trivia prizes simply because barely anyone else was around to answer (I’m pretty sure I got one of the questions wrong, and they just gave it to me). His style is undeniably distinctive, but Wes Anderson ( The Grand Budapest Hotel, The Phenoecian Scheme ) is far more understated than Waititi. In this one of Anderson’s two stop-motion animated films, a pandemic of “Snout Fever” spreads throughout the dogs of a futuristic Japan, who the mayor has exiled to an island made of trash. The first of these dogs to be exiled is the mayor’s ward, Atari’s, beloved bodyguard, Spots. Atari hijacks a plane to Trash Island in search of Spots, but crashes and is found by a group of disheveled canines: Boss ( Bill Murray , The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou ), Rex ( Edward Norton , Moonrise Kingdom ), King ( Bob Balaban , Moonrise Kingdom ), Duke ( Jeff Goldblum , The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou ) and Chief ( Bryan Cranston , Asteroid City ), the rowdiest of the bunch. Chief, who in a past life was a stray until he got put in the pound and was briefly adopted before biting the hand of his new owner’s child and escaping, is at first very wary of this new potential master. But after the rest of the group gets separated and Chief is left as Atari’s sole protector, he warms up to the boy and dedicates himself to finding Spots. Meanwhile at home, it is revealed that scientists have found a cure for Snout Fever, but the mayor is deliberately denying it so he can introduce his robotic hounds and even kills off the scientist who discovered it with poison wasabi. A teenage journalist, Tracy ( Greta Gerwig , Frances Ha ), develops a crush on the missing Atari from afar and starts to unravel the mayor’s conspiracy. Back on Trash Island, Atari gives the previously soot-black Chief a bath, revealing that he is truly white with black spots, just like Spots. When they finally find Spots, it is revealed that Chief and Spots came from the same litter, and Chief becomes Atari’s new bodyguard. Atari and his new entourage of dogs make it back home in time for the mayor’s announcement that all dogs on Trash Island will be executed, where he is confronted by Tracy and her pro-dog advocacy group, and the believed-to-be-dead Atari reads a haiku for the crowd: “Whatever happened / to man’s best friend? / Falling spring blossom.” The mayor is usurped, Atari becomes the new ruler and all of the dogs are cured. After watching these two films, I considered what parallels were between them. Both show young boys and their complicated relationship with corrupt rulers leading the battle against a needlessly oppressed group of people (or dogs). Both show the boys’ attempts to enter the war and win it, whether it’s for the side they were originally fighting for or not. Both show the boys form bonds with beings believed to be harmful beasts but who truly hold hearts of gold. More importantly than anything, though, they are both films that would be introduced to you by your friend’s shitty, pretentious boyfriend (it happened to me). I’m not one of those people who is annoying about this, but I love Wes Anderson and have seen all of his films. If I had to rank them all, though, Isle of Dogs would unfortunately be toward the bottom. Especially after the hilariously charming, heartwarming yet heartbreaking Jojo Rabbit , it just felt dry and sluggish. It’s also worth mentioning that with Jojo Rabbit , Waititi takes on the role of the man who tormented his ancestors to paint him as the raving lunatic that he was. Yet, I’m not really sure where Anderson’s choice to set Isle of Dogs in Japan came from. Jojo Rabbit wins the war. –Braxtyn Birrell Read more about this year’s SLFS Summer Showdowns: SLFS Summer Showdown: Hackers vs Tank Girl SLFS Summer Showdown: Phenomena vs The Last Unicorn To help SLUG continue highlighting events from local theaters, consider joining our community of donors! https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyz.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The body of Jang Mi-ran was found at a palm tree farm 500m from her home By Jake Kwon ,Â Seoul correspondent Â and Â Kelly Ng Published 26 August 2026, 08:01 BST Four missing people have been found dead on South Korean holiday island Jeju, as local police face mounting public criticism for allegedly mishandling missing persons cases. Reports emerged last week that authorities were launching a belated search for a woman reported missing months ago. This sparked criticism of the police for failing to search for her earlier. The scandal has since deepened with the arrest of a police sergeant, surnamed Bu, who is accused of lying to victims' families and prematurely closing missing persons cases. Four officers in the sergeant's chain of command have been put on administrative leave and on Tuesday President Lee Jae Myung ordered a sweeping reform of the police force. Since Saturday, police have found four bodies on the island, including that of 37-year-old Jang Mi-ran who had gone missing in May. On Monday, her body was located at a palm tree farm about 500 metres (547 yards) from where she was staying. She was believed to have killed herself. Bu is suspected to have closed Jang's case prematurely without confirming her whereabouts. According to local reports, Bu had allegedly told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to Jang over the phone and she had told Bu she did not wish to speak to her boyfriend. Police also found the body of a man in his 60s from Jeju City on Saturday. The man had gone missing on 28 June. Bu had closed his case and reportedly told the family that the man was found "safe" but "does not wish to disclose his location to the family". "We believed the police when they said my father was safe and waited, but after 51 days, what returned was his body," the man's son told reporters. It is not yet clear whether Bu was involved in the missing persons cases for two other bodies that were found in coastal villages in recent days. Police are now examining all the missing persons reports that Bu had handled, which number nearly 300. Jeju is one of South Korea's most popular tourist destinations. The island, known for its rows of palm trees and sparkling waters, received more than 13 million foreign and domestic visitors last year. While violent crime is rare in South Korea, suicide rates are among the highest in the world. Some experts have said the low crime rate is part of the reason why missing persons cases are not taken seriously. "After experiencing on the field that the absolute majority of missing adults are found quickly, [the officers] tend to assume all cases are like that," Lee Yung-hyeock, a professor specialising in police science at Konkuk University, told Yonhap news agency. While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Jeju, known for its sparkling waters, is a popular holiday destination in South Korea On Tuesday, President Lee said during a Cabinet meeting that "the recent breakdown in police discipline and irresponsibility in public safety matters have become serious problems". Pointing out that the police are likely to wield the most power out of all the state's institutions, he said "the Korean people are questioning whether [the police] deserve this large power". South Korea's national police chief was grilled by lawmakers at an emergency National Assembly hearing on Monday, during which he admitted that "there is a fault in the system". This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for South Korea's police. The government had recently passed reform to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics. However, the reform has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence. https://www.businessinsider.com/western-.text: SOUTHEASTERN UKRAINE — Two soldiers emerged from the tree line carrying the drone, trying to avoid scraping its wings against the branches. They placed it on the launch rail, angled toward the open sky above a field of budding sunflowers. The drone sprang to life, its small, rear-facing propeller roaring like a lawnmower. Sporadic raindrops pitter-pattered on the aircraft as the Ukrainian operators waited for their launch window. Then, at the press of a button, the drone shot into the gray sky for its final test flight before deployment to the front lines — where it would be sent to hunt. Drones have radically transformed the war in Ukraine. To capture how uncrewed aircraft are reshaping combat and how lessons from the fight are changing the way companies build these weapons, Business Insider followed a Western-made AR3 surveillance drone from its factory in Wales to the battlefield in southeastern Ukraine, where soldiers from the 15th Artillery Reconnaissance "Black Forest" Brigade readied it for front-line operations. Its journey from production to the front underscores one of the central dynamics defining both the conflict and Western military and industrial planning. Ukraine still needs foreign aircraft to sustain its fight, while Western manufacturers need Ukrainian combat experience to keep those aircraft relevant against evolving Russian defenses. There's a deeper lesson in the manufacturing-and-feedback loop as NATO braces for its own potential fight. Sarmat, a platoon commander in the Black Forest Brigade who requested to be identified only by his call sign for security reasons, said that although Ukraine can produce millions of drones each year, its forces still need more aircraft and combat capability than the country can supply on its own. With Western-supplied drones, he said, "we have the opportunity to fly more, to detect more, and to be much more successful." At a private airfield on the Welsh coast, factory workers assemble AR3 drones inside one of several manufacturing sites in Britain that are operated by the Portuguese defense company Tekever. The long World War II-era runway and private airspace around the quaint town of Cardigan make it an ideal location for flight testing. Many of the drones produced here will soon embark on a nearly 2,000-mile journey east to Ukraine. Before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Tekever made reconnaissance drones for governments and commercial clients to monitor illegal fishing and migration at sea. Now, the company is increasingly producing uncrewed aircraft for Ukraine. Check out our documentary At the start of the war, Ukraine relied heavily on Western military assistance to fend off Russia's invasion forces. Kyiv also invested heavily in its own drone industry to gain a technological advantage over a much larger military. Hundreds of Ukrainian companies now produce millions of aircraft annually, including strike and reconnaissance drones. That growth has reduced Ukraine's dependence on foreign suppliers for some types of drones, but it has not eliminated it. Longer-range reconnaissance aircraft such as the AR3 can fly deeper and stay aloft longer than many of the smaller, cheaper drones that Ukraine produces in vast numbers. These tools give commanders a key way to locate valuable Russian targets beyond the immediate front. Ukrainian drone production and battlefield tactics are also shaping Western military planning and training. Top NATO officials have said they are absorbing many lessons from the conflict, including how quickly drone designs and countermeasures become obsolete. Western support is "extremely important to Ukraine," said Scott McClelland, the deputy director of Tekever's defense unit. "This ultimately comes down to wider European security." The UK is one of the largest suppliers of military aid and security assistance to Ukraine. It has committed more than $21 billion in military support since 2022, including 150,000 strike, reconnaissance, and logistics drones this year. Tekever's AR3, the specific cost of which the company declined to provide, is among the systems supplied through that support, along with drones from British drone makers Windracers and Malloy Aeronautics. Sarmat's unit received its first AR3 in early 2024 and learned to operate the aircraft from Tekever. But the conversation doesn't end there. Tekever maintains a secure hotline around the clock to answer questions from Ukrainian operators. The soldiers, in turn, test new technology in combat and tell the company what needs to change to make the drone more effective. Exchanges like these between troops and industry have given rise to an accelerated development cycle driven by the brutal demands of modern warfare. A drone that works against Russian defenses today may struggle once Russia changes its jamming, detection, or interception tactics. Manufacturers must then modify the aircraft before the advantage disappears. McClelland said that the feedback from Ukraine allows Tekever to continually upgrade the drone. For instance, after the Black Forest Brigade requested a change to the AR3's climb rate, the company modified the engine. "The operating environment in Ukraine has really required us to respond at a speed that is almost alien to traditional Western procurement," McClelland said. Western militaries might spend years bringing a new product to life and putting it into service with the armed forces. For Ukraine, that would be "far, far too late," he said. Technology developed on that timeline could be "completely redundant" by the time it reached the battlefield because Russian forces and the conditions of the war would have already changed, creating new requirements. The pressure to move at speed and remain on the cutting edge extends beyond a single drone or type of drone. Western governments are studying how to shorten weapons development and procurement cycles for future conflicts in which equipment may need to be updated within months or weeks, rather than years. Ukraine is providing a real-time test of whether defense companies and procurement systems can keep pace. Business Insider reporters traveled across Ukraine to document how new technologies, tactics, and industries are radically changing warfare. Read more dispatches from Ukraine here: From Wales, the drones are boxed and sent to Portugal; then begins the long overland journey across Europe to Poland, where they cross into Ukraine. Tekever did not disclose specific shipping details for security reasons. After a drive from the factory in Wales to London, a flight to Warsaw, two trains to Kyiv, and a final drive to a remote forest at the end of a dirt road near Dnipro — more than 24 hours of movement east — Business Insider caught up with one of Tekever's drones. The Black Forest Brigade uses the forest as cover when setting up AR3 drones for operations. The soldiers had also strung up camouflage netting to conceal their position from Russian drones that could be nearby. They carried assault rifles and electronic-warfare equipment as a last line of defense. The soldiers pulled a box from a windowless van that had been driven from Portugal with their drone. The vehicle also served as the aircraft's ground-control station. Slightly beyond the tree line, the Ukrainians assembled a catapult launch rail and communications antennae, then put together the AR3 like a Lego set, piece by piece, and ran a number of pre-flight checks under the cover of their camouflage netting. After securing the aircraft on the rail and waiting for a light rain shower to pass, the operators received clearance to launch. The drone, powered by its gas engine, took off into the sky. A few minutes later, it deployed a parachute and floated down onto the field before landing on an airbag. Two soldiers scrambled across to retrieve it. This was only a test flight — a final check before a real mission against Russian forces. On an operational flight, the AR3 can remain airborne for hours. It typically operates dozens of miles behind the front lines, searching for high-value targets such as air defense systems, radars, and artillery, Sarmat said. Operators pass the coordinates they collect to artillery crews, who can then decide whether to engage. The drone can return later to conduct a battle damage assessment should offensive units opt to open fire. That work fills a critical gap between the smaller drones watching the immediate front and other surveillance systems looking much farther into Russian-held territory. Operational tempo is high. The team works nonstop, sometimes more than seven days without a rest. Summer is ideal for reconnaissance; cameras are less effective in the winter, and the unit doesn't fly in bad weather. "Every week, we have a lot of targets," Sarmat said. The battlefield has changed dramatically since the war began in 2022. It is now saturated with electronic warfare, which can disrupt flight operations for drones like the AR3 that rely on radio-frequency connections vulnerable to signal jamming. A drone does not need to be shot down to be rendered ineffective. If Russian forces sever its communications, interfere with its navigation, or expose the operator's position, the mission may fail and leave the crew at risk. Tekever declined to say how many of its AR3s have been lost in Ukraine. In August, Russian state media reported that Russian forces had downed an AR3 and transferred it to a research institute for study. Ukraine has been forced to explore innovative solutions to keep its drones in the sky. "It's war," Sarmat said. "Somebody has a shield — we create a sword. Then we create an automatic weapon. It's the same situation with electronic warfare." The work has become more dangerous for the Ukrainian operators. Every day, the drone-infested "kill zone" on the battlefield is expanding, putting even launch positions farther from the front within Russia's reach. That challenge can make concealment and mobility as important as the drones themselves at times. A sophisticated reconnaissance drone offers little advantage if Russian forces can find and attack the team launching it. Working from the forest is critical to the Black Forest Brigade's survival. Once, they lived in the trees for a month. Mid-range reconnaissance drones like the AR3 help Ukraine find Russian forces and equipment behind the front lines. But as Ukraine leverages these Western-made weapons in the war, there's a deeper lesson in the cooperation for NATO. For alliance countries preparing for a possible large-scale confrontation with Russia, the lesson isn't simply that their militaries need drones. They may also need factories, purchasing systems, and military institutions that can effectively act on front-line feedback, staying ahead of an adversary's swift adaptations. "Our main task is to win the war," Sarmat said. "But also, we have a task to give our partners all our experience and our advice on how to be successful on the front lines."

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Members of the White Australia party, including its leader, Thomas Sewell, sat in the front of the courtroom’s public benches. Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Members of the White Australia party, including its leader, Thomas Sewell, sat in the front of the courtroom’s public benches. Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The Guardian Australia news Ban on neo-Nazi White Australia party is ‘authoritarian’ and breaches constitution, high court hears Lawyers also argue commonwealth does not have the power to ban a political party, as the high court ruled in 1951 over attempt to ban the Communist party Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Basford Canales Tue 8 Sep 2026 03.49 EDT First published on Tue 8 Sep 2026 00.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Lawyers for an outlawed neo-Nazi political party have argued anti-hate laws passed after the Bondi terror attack rely on the opinion of a politician and are “authoritarian in nature”. The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May after the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation passed on its recommendation to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke. The listing means that activities including supporting, funding, training, recruiting and joining the group constitute a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison. The far-right nationalist party is challenging the ban at the high court over two days this week, with its lawyers arguing the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to Burke breaches the separation of powers. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Lawyers also argued the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling in 1951, which overturned a ban on the Communist party of Australia. If successful, the ruling could wind back the laws that have also banned the Islamist group Hizb ut-Tahrir. On Tuesday, the group’s barristers, Peter King and Shahed Sharify, argued a total ban on the party was akin to using a “sledgehammer on a nut”. The arguments centre on proving part 5.3B of the criminal code – which allows the federal police minister to recommend to the attorney general that a group is listed as a prohibited hate group – is invalid. Sharify argued the law’s breach of implied freedom of political communication was “authoritarian in nature” and suggested it could be used to ban any political party where its members had threatened or engaged in a hate crime with the assistance of the organisation. The barrister said the banning of hate groups was determined by a politician, based on an opinion with no judicial fairness to appeal that decision. Sharify said the law’s purposes would be better served by handing that decision to a judge rather than a “busy minister who flicks through a brief and decides in two hours”. Acting for the government, Brendan Lim, denied the laws could be used for the “illegitimate purpose of quelling political competition”. “It can’t happen,” he said. Groups can be listed if it is considered “reasonably necessary to protect the Australian community or part of the Australian community against social, psychological, physical or economic harm”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Under the rules, Burke must receive advice from the head of Asio recommending that an organisation be considered for listing. The home affairs minister must then receive written agreement from the attorney general and brief the opposition leader. Unlike the terrorist group listing, a listed hate group cannot make a de-listing application . The government is also expected to defend the anti-hate laws by arguing the party is not a political party but an arm of White Australia, itself a rebranded version of NSN. “Forming a political party was a calculated attempt to secure legal protection for members engaging in openly racist and anti-Semitic speech,” the commonwealth said in written submissions. Members of the White Australia party sat in the front of the courtroom’s public benches, including its leader, Tom Sewell . The 33-year-old was sentenced in June to a community corrections order – which includes 200 hours of community work – for behaving in an offensive manner in public. A Melbourne magistrate had found the neo-Nazi leader emulated “Nazi thugs of 1930s Berlin” when he used “appalling racial slurs” during a stunt outside a Chinese consulate. Disclaimer Links PAGES on NUCLEAR ISSUES Romania steps up efforts to restart Cernavoda nuclear reactors By Iulian Ernst in Bucharest August 24, 2026 , https://www.intellinews.com/romania-steps-up-efforts-to-restart-cernavoda-nuclear-reactors-462977/ Romanian authorities are changing their approach to restoring water levels at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant, with national waterways management company Apele Romane (Romanian Waters) building a temporary dam on the Danube and state-controlled hydropower group Hidroelectrica releasing additional water from its Olt River reservoirs to support the restart of at least one of the two reactors currently offline, according to G4Media and Radio Romania . The measures follow several weeks of emergency interventions that included dredging and attempts to sink barges loaded with stone in an effort to raise water levels near the nuclear plant’s intake. Those measures produced insufficient results, leaving Romania dependent on more expensive electricity imports during peak consumption hours. Under the revised strategy, Apele Romane is constructing a transverse guide dam on the Old Danube arm to redirect water towards the intake channel serving the plant. Emergency dredging is continuing in the Cernavoda area under the coordination of the Lower Danube River Administration and Apele Romane. Hidroelectrica has meanwhile started releasing additional water from reservoirs on the Olt River. According to Antena 3 , the company can release around 50 cubic metres per second for five days, although water reserves in the Olt system have also been reduced following several months of drought. The Ministry of National Defence has resumed support for the emergency works. Military specialists will carry out topobathymetric and geodetic measurements, while military divers will participate in underwater interventions. The effectiveness of the measures remains constrained by the exceptionally low flow of the Danube. Water entering Romania’s section of the river is currently around 1,300 cubic metres per second, roughly one-third of the multi-annual average. According to the forecast for August 22-29, the flow is expected to remain at around this level for the first three days before gradually increasing to approximately 1,550 cubic metres per second. The expected natural increase would therefore provide considerably more water than the temporary releases from the Olt reservoirs. The engineering works could eventually have a larger effect by improving the flow towards the nuclear plant’s intake, but their impact is unlikely to be sufficient immediately. This leaves the timing of a reactor restart dependent primarily on the availability of adequate cooling water. Cernavoda’s two reactors, each with an installed capacity of 680 MW, have been taken offline because of insufficient Danube water for cooling. Their prolonged outage has increased Romania’s reliance on electricity imports during a period of high summer consumption. Out of the 7,500 MW consumed by Romania during the peak hours, it imports 1,00-2,500 MW. https://www.politico.eu/article/totalene.text: WINCHESTER, England — TotalEnergies refused fuel to helicopters evacuating civilians as Islamist militants overran the Mozambican town of Palma in 2021 and later denied British special forces use of its nearby construction site for a rescue mission, a British inquest heard this week. The four-day hearing in Winchester was a coroner’s inquest, a British judicial proceeding to establish how and why Philip Mawer — a 58-year-old British construction contractor working on the French energy giant’s gas plant project — was killed by a rocket-propelled grenade while fleeing the assault. The claims emerged in testimony and evidence presented during the hearing; the coroner did not, however, find that TotalEnergies’ decisions affected rescue efforts, saying Mawer’s security was the sole responsibility of his employer, a Dubai-based contractor, and the hotel at which he stayed. Advertisement Advertisement Coroner Jason Pegg ruled on Thursday that Mawer was unlawfully killed by an unknown person, but accepted an argument by lawyers from TotalEnergies’ Mozambican subsidiary that the company had no legal duty of care to him because he was a subcontractor. The testimony could carry consequences in France, where TotalEnergies faces two criminal complaints over its Mozambique operations , including an involuntary manslaughter case tied to the deaths of contractors during the Palma attack. A French investigating magistrate was appointed last year to examine that complaint. “These hearings were crucial, crucial, crucial,” said Henri Thulliez, a French human rights lawyer who filed both criminal complaints in Paris and who was in Winchester to watch proceedings. “Finally, we have people talking under oath about what happened in Palma. It’s very important, and very rare when it comes to accountability for multinationals.” Thulliez’s second complaint accuses TotalEnergies of complicity in war crimes and torture. It alleges the energy giant became an accomplice in a massacre — first reported by POLITICO — in which Mozambican soldiers brutalized, starved, suffocated, executed or disappeared around 200 men at the company's gatehouse from June to September 2021. TotalEnergies has denied responsibility for the deaths during the ISIS attack, which killed 1,354 civilians, including 55 people working on the TotalEnergies project, according to a house-to-house survey carried out by POLITICO. In response to questions from POLITICO, it acknowledged in 2024 that “a small number” of project workers had been stationed outside its secure compound during the attack and exposed to the bloodbath. In 2025, the company — through its subsidiary Mozambique LNG — told POLITICO it had no knowledge of the gatehouse killings, adding that its “extensive research” had “not identified any information nor evidence that would corroborate the allegations of severe abuses and torture.” Advertisement Advertisement In response to a request for comment for this article, TotalEnergies referred POLITICO to its previous statements. The coroner’s court heard that Mawer, country manager for Dubai-based contractor RA International, was in northern Mozambique helping build TotalEnergies’ gas project near Palma — an area that had been subject to Islamist attacks since 2017. By March 2021, rebels had cut land access to the project and the town. TotalEnergies evacuated its own staff and allowed 700 Mozambican soldiers to deploy inside its fortified concession, while thousands of contractors and subcontractors remained in Palma, living in hotels protected by guards with wooden batons and protected around town by a few dozen soldiers and policemen. When militants attacked the town on March 24, Mawer took shelter in a hotel with 182 other people. On March 26, after two days trapped at the hotel, Mawer fled in a convoy. A rocket-propelled grenade struck his vehicle, killing him. The inquest heard that two members of Britain’s Special Air Service flew from Kenya to Mozambique intending to rescue Mawer. Francesca Wiley, a lawyer representing Mawer’s family, told the court that the SAS was denied permission to use TotalEnergies’ site. While debating their next move on March 27, the SAS were informed that Mawer was already dead. The inquest also heard that TotalEnergies refused to supply fuel to helicopters operated by South African private military contractor Dyck Advisory Group, which was evacuating civilians from Palma. DAG chief Max Dyck said the lack of fuel limited the rescue effort. “Could we have saved a lot more people?” Dyck testified. “Definitely.” Advertisement Advertisement TotalEnergies’ Mozambican subsidiary was represented by lawyer Adam Payter. He argued that Mawer was a subcontractor who was not formally under the company’s protection and for whom it had no evacuation plan. Mawer’s brothers, Bill and Mark, accused TotalEnergies of abandoning him. “Why did Total refuse fuel and landing rights to the helicopter evacuation effort?” they said in a statement after the hearing. “Why was our brother allowed to die so close to a protected compound and a substantial military force?” At the inquest, Detective Chief Inspector Patrick Allen of Britain’s SO15 counterterrorism command said a death toll of 1,402 was consistent with his unit’s own investigation. He also agreed with Mawer’s lawyer, Wiley, when she described the Palma assault as the “second biggest terror attack of all time, after 9/11.”
